target_audience: Advanced High School Students (AP Calculus) or University Freshmen

sections.title: Introduction: Explicit vs. Implicit Functions
sections.content: Begin by contrasting functions we know ($y = x^2$) with complex curves where $y$ is 'tangled' with $x$. Visually demonstrate that while some curves are hard to solve for $y$, they still have slopes. Introduce the concept: $y$ is a 'secret' function of $x$.
sections.example: Visual comparison: A straight line $y = 2x + 1$ (Explicit) vs. a perfect circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ (Implicit). An animation shows a point moving around the circle, highlighting its changing tangent slope.

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: The Chain Rule Power-Up
sections.content: Recall the Chain Rule: $d/dx [f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$. Crucially, explain that when we differentiate $y$ with respect to $x$, we must treat $y$ as an inner function. This is the 'secret sauce' of implicit differentiation.
sections.example: Animation: Differentiating $[f(x)]^2$ results in $2f(x) \cdot f'(x)$. Then, swap $f(x)$ with the letter $y$ to show $d/dx(y^2) = 2y \cdot (dy/dx)$.

sections.title: The Three-Step Recipe
sections.content: Present a clear 3-step logical flow: 1. Differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x$ (remembering the chain rule for $y$ terms). 2. Collect all terms containing $dy/dx$ on one side. 3. Factor out $dy/dx$ and solve.
sections.example: A 'Recipe Card' graphic appears on screen with icons for 'Differentiate', 'Collect', and 'Isolate'.

sections.title: Worked Example: The Circle's Slope
sections.content: Apply the steps to the equation of a circle. Show how the $x$ terms behave normally, while the $y$ terms spawn a $dy/dx$ 'tag'. Graphically show how the resulting formula $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}$ perfectly predicts the slope at any point $(x, y)$.
sections.example: Solve $x^2 + y^2 = 25$. Step 1: $2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0$. Step 2: $2y(dy/dx) = -2x$. Step 3: $dy/dx = -x/y$. Visual: At point $(3, 4)$, the slope is $-3/4$.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Robotic Laser
sections.content: Apply the concept to a mechanical device. Imagine a robotic arm (character: 'Robo-A') programmed to follow an elliptical path. To ensure the laser cuts precisely, we need to know the 'instantaneous direction' (the derivative) at any coordinate without re-programming the whole equation.
sections.example: Robo-A follows the path $4x^2 + 9y^2 = 36$. Use implicit differentiation to find the slope at $(0, 2)$ to show why the laser points horizontally at the peak of the ellipse.

sections.title: Summary & Key Takeaway
sections.content: Recap: Implicit differentiation is a shortcut that saves us from messy algebra. Whenever you see $y$, treat it as a function $y(x)$ and 'tag' its derivative with $dy/dx$.
sections.example: A quick visual montage of various curves (Folium of Descartes, Ellipses) all being 'solved' by the same universal method.
